sentences.text: I remember the linoleum sticking to my socks as I stood behind his chair, reading over his shoulder about Normandy hedgerows. You could hear the loader's routine in his cadence — shell, breech, ready — even sixty years after his last fight. Cracked at the spine, the album fell open to the page where his memoir began, the ink faded but the handwriting steady. Snapshots of five grinning boys on an armored hull; only one of them made it home to Ohio. We leaned closer whenever his voice dropped, because the quiet parts were always about the crew he'd lost outside Aachen. After the last page he closed the album gently, patted its cover twice, and asked who wanted more pie. His memoir never brags; it just lists the towns, the mud, and the boys who drove through both. He'd been a gunner, he told us, and the periscope's narrow world was all he saw of France. Nobody touched the pie while he described the night his platoon crossed the Roer under artillery. "Read the part about Sergeant Malone again," my cousin begged, elbows on the table, homework forgotten. Turret markings, bogie wheels, a crooked antenna — he named every part of the machine in that photograph like an old friend. He read the roster of his old crew slowly, pausing after each name as if waiting for someone at the table to answer. Every November the ritual repeats: the album comes down from the shelf, the kitchen goes quiet, and the war returns in his careful voice. Forty years of silence, and now the whole story spilling out over cold coffee. The memoir's third chapter, read aloud between bites of pie, described repairing a thrown track in freezing mud while shells walked the treeline. Did anyone else notice how his hands shook when he turned to the page with the burned-out hulls? Grandpa flattened the album on the kitchen table and tapped a photo of his Sherman, its turret scrawled with a name nobody could read anymore. Was it strange, my mother asked him, to sleep inside thirty tons of steel while the world burned? Folded into the back cover, a battalion newsletter still listed reunion dates from 1987. My sister kept the tape recorder running under a dish towel so his stories wouldn't vanish like the men in the pictures. He counted the corydoras twice, then a third time, before finding the missing one dozing inside the ceramic cave. Rinse new gravel until the runoff turns clear, or the filter will choke on silt for days. We'll cure the new driftwood in a bucket for a week so the tannins don't turn everything amber. Somewhere behind the heater cord, the bristlenose pleco rasped at the glass, leaving faint clean trails through the algae film. By lamplight the neon tetras schooled tighter, a shivering blue thread behind the driftwood. Ammonia at zero, nitrite at zero, nitrates creeping toward forty — time for a thirty-percent water change. At lights-out the betta flares at his own reflection in the darkened glass. Condensation fogged the glass lid, and beneath it the amazon swords pearled tiny silver beads of oxygen. "Guppies again?" she sighed, netting the newest batch of fry out of the filter chamber. You'd think snails were decorative until a hundred of them mob one sinking algae wafer. A thermometer suctioned crooked to the glass has read 78 degrees, steady, since Tuesday. Overnight the heater's indicator blinked orange, then quit, and by dawn the water had slid to 68 degrees. Every Sunday she tops off the aquarium with dechlorinated water warmed to match the glass. Honestly, the sponge filter's bubbling puts me to sleep faster than any white-noise app ever did. Her evening routine: lights dimmed at nine, a pinch of flakes, ten quiet minutes watching the angelfish drift. The siphon hose bucked in my hand until gravel dust clouded the bucket like weak tea. Water changes go faster now that the python hooks straight to the kitchen faucet. During the blackout he floated hand warmers in a zip bag to keep the fry from chilling. Was the filter intake supposed to rattle like that, or had a pebble slipped past the guard? Feed sparingly on Fridays; whatever the platies miss will rot beneath the sword plants by morning. What is the meaning of the word tank?
